text.en: In a small school garden we find grass, a neem tree, ants, a butterfly and a frog. Each is different. Why are there so many kinds of living things, and how can we group them?

Diversity means variety. Earth has a huge variety of plants and animals in forests, deserts, oceans and cities. Living things differ in size, shape, colour and where they live.
We can group plants by what they look like. Herbs usually have soft, non-woody stems. Shrubs often have several woody stems close to the ground. A tree usually has one main woody trunk. Climbers need support to climb up. Creepers spread along the ground. Plants can also be grouped by leaves, flowers, roots and stems.
Animals can be grouped by what they eat: herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals, omnivores eat both. Animals can be grouped by where they live: on land, in water or both, like frogs, which are amphibians. Some animals have a backbone (vertebrates, such as fish, birds and mammals) and some do not (invertebrates, such as insects and worms).
A feature that helps a living thing survive in its surroundings is an adaptation. A camel stores fat in its hump and can go many days without water. A fish has gills and fins for living in water. Many cacti have thick stems that store water and leaves modified into spines. These are features of many cacti, rather than rules for every plant in a desert.
Grouping helps us study and remember so many living things. Grouping can show shared features. Scientists look for more than one shared feature when they work out how living things are related.

Imagine making a list of living things you notice in the school garden. Walk slowly on the path. Observe plants and animals without picking leaves or handling the animals.

board.text: Garden record: place, time and living things

text.en: Twelve ants of the same kind are twelve individuals, but they add only one kind to a list of the garden’s diversity. A butterfly and a grass plant add other kinds.

board.text: Individuals and kinds are different counts

text.en: When you finish, say which living things you saw during that visit. A second visit may reveal kinds you missed, especially if you return at a different time of day.
To decide whether you are seeing a herb, shrub or tree, look closely at the stems. A young neem tree can be short, but it can still grow into a tree with a main woody trunk.

board.text: Look at the stem and growth form

text.en: A soft-stemmed mint plant fits the herb group. A rose usually has several woody branches close to the base, so it is a useful example of a shrub.

board.text: Rose: woody branches near the base

text.en: Compare drawings of a grass leaf and a hibiscus leaf. In the grass leaf, many veins run side by side. In the hibiscus leaf, the smaller veins form a netlike pattern.

board.text: Grass leaf: veins run side by side

text.en: Both leaves can be green. The veins give you a feature you can sketch and compare even when colour does not help.

board.text: Choose a feature you can compare

text.en: Look at an adult frog near the edge of a pond. It may rest on land and swim in water. A crow usually uses land and trees, but both the crow and the frog have a backbone.

board.text: Habitat and backbone are different rules

text.en: A butterfly can share the garden with a crow. It belongs in a different group when the rule is backbone, because the butterfly has no backbone and the crow does.
If you group the same animals by food, you may get different groups. A crow can eat grains and insects. A cow mostly eats plants, and an adult frog usually eats insects and other small animals.

board.text: Food rule: plant, animal, or both

text.en: Fish gills take in oxygen dissolved in water, while fins help a fish move and steer. A duck also swims, but it must breathe air with lungs. Swimming alone does not tell you how an animal breathes.
In many cacti, the thick stem holds water and the spines take the place of broad leaves. Think of how these features help the plant where water is limited.

board.text: Cactus: water stored in the stem

text.en: A camel’s hump stores fat, which the camel can use for energy. Its broad feet also help spread its weight over sand. These are two different features useful in the same habitat.

board.text: Broad feet: spread weight on sand

text.en: A habitat gives living things the conditions and resources they need. A pond provides water for fish, while plants at its edge can offer places where small animals hide.

board.text: Habitats provide water, food and shelter

text.en: When part of a habitat changes, ask which living things might be affected. If the shallow edge of a pond dries, animals using that edge may lose cover or access to water.
Try two ways of grouping a crow, a butterfly and a cow. First compare which of them have a backbone. Then compare which have wings. Notice that the groups change.
The crow and cow share a backbone. The crow and butterfly both have wings. Say the rule when you describe a group so others know why you put the living things together.

problem.en: Group a tiger, a cow, a crow and an adult frog by what each usually eats.

text.en: Tiger eats flesh, so it is a carnivore.
A cow eats plants, a crow eats plant and animal foods, and an adult frog usually eats insects and other small animals. So the cow is a herbivore, the crow an omnivore, and the adult frog a carnivore.

why.en: Use the same food rule for all four animals.

prompt.en: Explain why a cactus can live in a desert.

requiredIdeas.en: It stores water in its stem.
In many cacti, spines replace broad leaves, reducing how much water is lost through leaves.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all plants need lots of water.

points.en: Diversity means variety of living things.
Plants group as herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers and creepers.
Animals group by food, habitat and backbone.
